title: If ... not and unless; if and whether; etc.
subtitle: unless you have a reservation / whether or not
summary: Decide when unless can replace if ... not, and when only whether will do instead of if.

lesson.heading: unless = 'except if'
lesson.text: **Unless** is used in conditional sentences with the meaning 'except if'. With unless we use present tenses when we talk about the future.

examples.text: You can't travel on this train **unless** you have a reservation.
**Unless it rains**, I'll pick you up at six.

lesson.heading: unless or if ... not?
lesson.text: In real conditional sentences we can often use either **unless** or **if ... not** with a similar meaning. Unless carries an 'only if' implication.

examples.text: **Unless** the theatre is able to raise £100,000, it will have to close.
examples.note: or If the theatre isn't able to ...; it will close only if it can't raise the money

lesson.heading: Three places where only if ... not works
lesson.text: We use **if ... not** but not *unless* when the main clause says that the event in the if-clause is unexpected, usually in questions, and when the 'only if' implication does not apply.

examples.note: the main clause marks it as unexpected

examples.text: **If** you **don't** pass the test, what will you do?
**If** it **wasn't** the best performance of Hamlet I've seen, it was certainly the strangest.

left.label: Positive main clause - use if ... not
examples: **If I weren't** so tired, I'd give you a hand.
not Unless I were so tired ...

right.label: Negative main clause - unless is possible
examples: She **wouldn't** have gone to university **unless** her parents had insisted.

lesson.heading: if or whether
lesson.text: We can use **if** or **whether** to say that two possibilities have been talked or thought about, or that people are not sure about something.

examples.text: They couldn't decide **if** / **whether** it was worth resitting the exam.
Do you know **if** / **whether** Ben's at home?

left.label: whether - or not can follow immediately
examples: I didn't know **whether or not** Aya was coming.
or ... whether Aya was coming or not ...

right.label: if - or not only at the end
examples: I didn't know **if** Aya was coming **or not**.
not ... if or not Aya was coming

lesson.heading: whether rather than if
lesson.text: We use **whether** after a preposition (though *if* is sometimes used informally), before a to-infinitive, and in the pattern noun / adjective + **as to whether** meaning 'about' or 'concerning'.

examples.text: We argued about **whether** butter or margarine was better for you.
I couldn't decide **whether to buy** apples or bananas.
There was some disagreement **as to whether** he was eligible to play for France.

lesson.note: Also with as to whether: conflict, confusion, debate, discussion, doubt, question, speculation, uncertainty; concerned, indifferent, uncertain, undecided, unsure.

lesson.heading: Verbs and clause positions that prefer whether
lesson.text: We prefer **whether** after advise, choose, consider, depend on, discuss, talk about and think about, and in a clause acting as a subject or a complement.

examples.text: You should consider **whether** the car you are interested in is good value.
**Whether** the minister will quit over the issue remains to be seen.
The first issue is **whether** he knew he was committing a crime.

exercises.prompt: Unless it ___, I'll pick you up at six.
exercises.explanation: After unless we use a present tense to talk about the future, never will.

exercises.prompt: Match each unless clause with its main clause.

pairs.left: Unless the train leaves within five minutes,
pairs.right: we'll never get to the meeting.

pairs.left: Unless alternative sources of funding are found,
pairs.right: the research will not be able to continue.

pairs.left: Unless the roads have changed in that part of town,
pairs.right: I'm sure I'll be able to find my way there.

pairs.left: Unless the weather starts improving soon,
pairs.right: the farmers will lose their crops.
I think I'll buy that painting.

pairs.left: Unless you have been unemployed for six months,
pairs.right: you are not entitled to state benefit.

exercises.statement: Unless the infection is treated urgently, there is a real danger that she will die.
exercises.explanation: Correct. 'If the infection isn't treated' is also possible here.

exercises.prompt: It'll be surprising if Anya ___ her piano exam.
exercises.explanation: The main clause marks the event as unexpected, so unless is not possible.

exercises.prompt: ___ so clumsy, he'd be the best person to do the work.
exercises.explanation: In an unreal conditional with a positive main clause we use if ... not, not unless.

exercises.statement: Unless she had gone to university, she would have gone into the army.
exercises.explanation: If she hadn't gone to university, she would have gone into the army. The main clause is positive, so unless doesn't work.

exercises.statement: She wouldn't have gone to university unless her parents had insisted.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Unless is possible in an unreal conditional when the main clause is negative.

exercises.prompt: ___ a loan from the bank, how will you pay for the house?
exercises.explanation: We use if ... not rather than unless in questions.

exercises.prompt: She was undecided as to ___ to fly or go by train.
exercises.explanation: Only whether can come after a preposition-like as to and before a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: I didn't know ___ Aya was coming.
exercises.explanation: Only whether can be followed immediately by or not.

exercises.prompt: Does the gap take whether only, or would if work as well?

items.text: I was wondering ___ you'd had your exam results yet.
Have you any idea ___ Steve will be at the meeting?
Can you remember ___ the door was open or closed when you got to the house?
Police have refused to confirm ___ or not they have arrested anyone for the theft.
There was considerable debate as to ___ chess was a game or a sport.
The government is considering ___ to hold an enquiry into the accident.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence beginning with a whether-clause as subject.
exercises.answer: Whether the minister will quit over the issue remains to be seen.
exercises.explanation: A clause acting as the subject of a sentence begins with whether, not if.
